name: Difference Blend Header
summary: A fixed header whose every glyph inverts in real time against whatever scrolls beneath it — pale ground, ink ground, saturated ground, even mid-glyph on a split. No scrim, no class swapping, no JavaScript.

attempts.prompt: Build a fixed header that stays readable over any content that scrolls under it.
attempts.problem: Added a translucent dark scrim behind the header. That is the solution everyone ships and it is a compromise twice over: it dims the content the user is trying to look at, and it still fails over a mid-tone image where neither white nor dark text has enough contrast. It also has to be tuned by hand per site.

attempts.prompt: Use mix-blend-mode: difference on the header text instead.
attempts.problem: Put mix-blend-mode on the header while leaving it a background colour, so the header blended with its own background rather than the page behind it and nothing appeared to happen. Removing the background revealed the second problem: with no isolation on a wrapper, the blend reached the whole page stacking context, so the header inverted against unrelated content and other elements were dragged into the blending group.

finalPrompt:
Build a fixed header that stays readable over any content, in plain HTML and CSS with no JavaScript at all.

Use mix-blend-mode: difference on the header, with the text colour set to white. Difference against white inverts whatever is behind each pixel, which is what produces dark glyphs on a pale ground and pale glyphs on a dark one, per pixel and in real time.

Two rules make it work, and both are what people get wrong.

First: the header must have no background of its own. A background becomes the thing it blends with, so the effect silently does nothing. The content behind it has to be the backdrop.

Second: put isolation: isolate on the containing wrapper. Without it the blend participates in the page's root stacking context, reaching content it should not touch and pulling other elements into the blending group. The isolation defines exactly what the header is allowed to invert against.

Demonstrate it against four grounds in a scroll-snapping container: the page background, solid ink, a saturated accent, and a hard diagonal split so a single line of text visibly inverts differently along its own length. The split is the case that proves it is per-pixel rather than per-element.

Set pointer-events: none on the bar and restore it on the links, so the header never intercepts clicks meant for the content.

Under forced-colors: active the backdrop the effect depends on is gone, so opt out with mix-blend-mode: normal and fall back to Canvas and CanvasText on a solid bar.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties for the panels: var(--bg), var(--text), var(--accent), var(--accent-fg), var(--text-dim), var(--border). The header's own white is the blend operand, not a design colour.
why:
This is two CSS declarations and almost nobody ships it, which makes it the clearest case in the library of a technique lost to a single bad first encounter. Both failures are the same shape: the effect appears to do nothing, so people conclude it does not work and add a scrim.

Naming the two causes explicitly — a background defeats it, and without isolation it escapes — is the entire difference between a working component and an abandoned experiment. Neither is discoverable by staring at the code, because the failure mode is silence rather than an error.

The split-ground panel earns its place as the demo: it is the only one that proves the inversion happens per pixel rather than per element, and it is what makes someone want the component rather than merely understand it.
